content: Cutaneous drug eruptions are the most common type of adverse drug reactions, with the majority being allergic in origin. Morbilliform Rash Morbilliform rash is the most frequent type of cutaneous drug eruption. It resembles a measles-like viral exanthem. These rashes typically begin in dependent areas of the body and then spread to become generalized. They usually appear 2 to 10 days after starting the drug but can also occur up to 14 days after the drug has been discontinued. Urticaria Urticaria, which may be associated with angioedema, can result from drug therapy. It presents as transient, raised, red, pruritic, and well-demarcated lesions that resolve without leaving scars or hyperpigmentation. Erythema Multiforme Erythema multiforme minor is a cutaneous eruption that may initially resemble urticaria. The lesions are red, raised, and well-demarcated plaques that persist for several days to weeks. Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) Toxic epidermal necrolysis shares features with Stevens-Johnson syndrome, including the types of causative drugs, fever, mucosal membrane involvement, and full-thickness epidermal sloughing. DRESS Syndrome DRESS syndrome (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms) is a drug-induced hypersensitivity reaction. It is characterized by delayed-onset fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytosis, and visceral involvement, most commonly affecting the kidneys, liver, and/or heart. Leukocytoclastic Vasculitis Leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LV) is a hypersensitivity reaction marked by neutrophilic inflammation of blood vessels in the skin. Contact Dermatitis Allergic contact dermatitis can occur with various topical therapeutic agents, such as neomycin, benzocaine, and diphenhydramine. The skin eruption is characterized by asymmetrically distributed, erythematous, pruritic papules and vesicles, resembling acute eczematous dermatitis. This reaction typically appears 24 to 72 hours after exposure in previously sensitized individuals. Allergic contact dermatitis to topical medications is a type IV, T-cell-mediated response, also known as delayed-type hypersensitivity. Fixed Drug Eruption A fixed drug eruption is a less common type of drug-induced cutaneous reaction. It presents as a solitary erythematous macule during treatment with agents such as tetracycline, phenolphthalein (a laxative), NSAIDs, or other drugs. The macule is pruritic and evolves into a raised plaque or even a blister. These plaques are typically 2 to 4 cm in diameter. A skin biopsy can aid in diagnosis. Photosensitive Drug Eruption Photosensitive drug eruptions occur exclusively on sun-exposed skin. Depending on the type of photosensitizing drug, the reaction may be phototoxic or photoallergic. Phototoxic reactions (seen with sulfonamides, tetracyclines, and psoralens) involve the absorption of ultraviolet radiation, leading to energy release that damages epidermal cells. Clinically, this manifests as an exaggerated sunburn, though other morphologies, such as bullous eruptions and hyperpigmentation, can also occur. Photoallergic reactions (seen with griseofulvin, thiazides, and chlorpromazine) occur when ultraviolet energy causes the drug hapten to bind to native proteins on epidermal cells, forming a complete antigen that sensitizes nearby lymphocytes. This results in a pruritic, eczematous eruption on sun-exposed areas. After discontinuing the drug, re-exposure to sunlight may trigger a recurrence of the rash in photoallergic reactions but not in phototoxic eruptions.
